name: Vigilius of Rome
knownFor: Bishop of Rome from 537 to 555, made pope in place of Silverius, who was held at Constantinople through the quarrel over the Three Chapters and the council of 553, first defending them and then condemning them.
dates: Made pope in 537, when Belisarius removed Silverius (the continuation of Marcellinus's chronicle and the Book of the Popes; Procopius gives no year). Taken from Rome in 544 or 545, by Louise Loomis's date. Died in Sicily on his way home; a record of the time that Loomis reports gives 7 June 555, and Henry Percival gives the end of 554 or the start of 555
place: Rome; Constantinople from about 547; Sicily, where he died
role: Bishop of Rome; before that a Roman deacon and the pope's envoy at Constantinople

keyWorks.title: Constitutum on the Three Chapters
keyWorks.about: dated at Constantinople on 14 May 553, by Otto Guenther's reading, while the council sat without him; it condemns propositions drawn from Theodore of Mopsuestia but will not condemn Theodore himself, Theodoret of Cyrrhus or Ibas of Edessa by name, and forbids any further dispute over them

keyWorks.title: Letter to Eutychius of Constantinople (the Decretal Letter)
keyWorks.about: dated 8 December, which Henry Percival reckons as 553; it condemns the Three Chapters and cancels whatever Vigilius or others had said in their defence, citing Augustine of Hippo, who corrected his own writings

keyWorks.title: Judicatum
keyWorks.about: issued in 548, by Loomis's account, condemning the Three Chapters while holding to the Council of Chalcedon, and later withdrawn; the text itself is not in the sources used here

traces: The council of 553 condemned the Three Chapters in spite of his Constitutum, and he then accepted its ruling. Percival says the council was opposed across the West, with Milan in schism until 571 and a schism in Istria that lasted until 700.
Loomis says the quarrel over the Three Chapters brought a new schism between East and West, "which lasted seventy years".
remembered: The Book of the Popes gives a hostile life of him: the Romans call him a murderer, the crowd stones his ship, and he is dragged from an altar at Constantinople. Loomis judges that last account partly legendary.

Liberatus of Carthage and Victor of Tunnuna, both defenders of the Three Chapters, tell how he won the see through the empress Theodora. Theodor Mommsen says both hated him "iusto odio", with just hatred, and calls him perhaps the worst among bad popes.

uncertain: The scene of his leaving Rome comes from the Book of the Popes, whose life of him is hostile. Loomis finds that life full of mistakes and the scene told nowhere else. Louis Duchesne, whom Loomis follows, argues its author wrote no earlier than the time of Pope Pelagius the Second, who began in 579.

How he became pope. Procopius of Caesarea says only that Belisarius appointed him after sending Silverius away. Liberatus says the empress Theodora had him promise in secret to set aside Chalcedon and offered him money; Victor of Tunnuna says she drew a secret written pledge from him. Both are hostile to him, by Mommsen's judgment.

The letter in which he tells Theodosius of Alexandria, Anthimus of Constantinople and Severus of Antioch that he shares their faith. Liberatus and Victor copy it. Loomis, citing Duchesne, holds it must be a forgery unless Vigilius was a shameless double-dealer; Mommsen leaves open whether it is his or forged, and says it was taken as genuine at the time.

The death of Silverius. Liberatus, as Loomis translates him, says Silverius was handed to Vigilius's guards and starved on an island; the Book of the Popes says only that he was exiled and died a confessor. Loomis judges the guilt to rest partly on Vigilius.
Whether the letter to Eutychius is genuine. Percival reports that Jean Hardouin thought Garnier had proved it a forgery, and says the learned have generally accepted it.
The year of his death: 7 June 555 in the record of the time Loomis reports, the end of 554 or the start of 555 in Percival.
